archetype.name: Pocket Passer (intermediate attacker)
archetype.definition: A rhythm thrower who does almost nothing with his legs and wins from the pocket by hitting the 10-19 yard window, now more often into tight coverage than at any point in his Detroit years.

report.headline: Goff's aggressive intermediate attack has him at his 2024 peak, with zero picks.
report.take:
Goff is the same player he has been for a decade: a pocket passer with no rushing value (15 yards on 12 carries, and his designed runs have cost points). What has changed is how much he is willing to challenge coverage. His aggressiveness, the share of throws into tight windows, is 20.18% after 12.5% last year and roughly 11-13% every season since 2017. That shows up in the results. His 0.317 EPA per dropback ranks 4th of 45, essentially level with his 2024 season (0.293, 4th), and well above last year's 0.157 (16th).

The engine is the intermediate level. On 58 throws between 10 and 19 air yards he is at 0.929 EPA per attempt with a 62% success rate, and his 10+ yard throws as a group add up to more EPA than all of his dropbacks combined. Everything underneath, screens and checkdowns included, is roughly break-even. His accuracy hasn't really improved: CPOE of 1.26 ranks 20th, about where he usually sits. So the jump comes from where he is throwing and to whom. Sam LaPorta (0.847 EPA per target) and Jameson Williams (0.603) have been far more productive per look than Amon-Ra St. Brown, who still gets the most volume.

The numbers hide two things. First, zero interceptions on 223 attempts is not who he is. He threw 8 last year and 12 in each of 2023 and 2024, and he is throwing into tighter windows than he did then. The dossier also charts six turnover-worthy fumbles, so the ball-security record is better than the play. Second, the volume is partly a product of a defense that ranks 31st in EPA allowed. Every game but the Green Bay one went over the total, and the 412-yard day at Carolina came in a loss. When the Lions have needed a drive in a tight game, the production has thinned: third down sits at -0.109 EPA with a 35.7% conversion rate, and close fourth-quarter snaps are flat.

Where it heads: the efficiency looks real enough to stay in the top tier, because the intermediate game and LaPorta's usage are features of the offense rather than luck. The per-game yardage lead and the clean interception line will both come down. Some of that starts this week against a Minnesota defense that ranks first in essentially everything.

strengths.title: Owning the 10-19 yard window
strengths.body: His intermediate throws produce 0.929 EPA per attempt and carry the offense. It's the classic Goff play-action and timing game, pushed a little further downfield this year. Because it is built on scheme and route design rather than hot accuracy (his CPOE there is barely above zero), it should hold up. Expect the rate to drift down, but not collapse.

strengths.title: New willingness to throw tight windows
strengths.body: Aggressiveness is up 7.7 points on last year, a clear break from a decade of conservative tendencies. So far it has been all upside: more chunk plays and no interceptions. It looks like a deliberate change, and the efficiency it buys is likely to persist even when the picks arrive.

strengths.title: LaPorta and Williams as efficiency drivers
strengths.body: LaPorta's 0.847 EPA per target and Williams' 0.603 give Goff two targets who turn intermediate and deep looks into big gains. St. Brown carries the volume, but these two create the explosive value. LaPorta's rate is extreme and will cool, but the role is sound.

concerns.title: Interception-free line won't last
concerns.body: Zero interceptions while throwing into more tight windows than ever runs against his entire career. He threw 8 picks even in a quieter 2025. Add six turnover-worthy fumbles and the turnover luck is running hot. This is the most certain regression on the card.

concerns.title: Third downs are a weak spot
concerns.body: On third down, with 7.5 yards to go on average, he is below zero in EPA, converts only 35.7% and completes well under expectation. The big early-down plays are covering for an offense that stalls once it is behind the sticks. That matters most against defenses that win on early downs.

concerns.title: Volume tied to a leaky defense
concerns.body: Detroit's defense ranks 31st in EPA, which has forced shootouts and inflated his yardage. That is a product of game script, not a flaw in Goff, but his league-leading yards per game rests on it. A better defensive opponent or a low-scoring script takes it away.

trend.note: After a modest opener (206 yards), he has been consistently efficient. His last three games match his season EPA per dropback almost exactly, and the five-game stretch from Week 2 is slightly better. The only drift is a dip in CPOE, offset by more yards per attempt.

nextGame.headline: The league's best defense meets him without his usual shootout script
nextGame.body:
Minnesota ranks first in defensive EPA, pass EPA, success rate, hit rate and sack rate. It allows the fewest fantasy points to quarterbacks, and it ranks 7th against the deep ball and 4th on short throws. It also takes away LaPorta's role: no defense has been stingier per play against tight ends. The one soft spot is WR1, at 0.43 EPA per target (24th), which points straight at St. Brown. Opponents have passed far less than normal against the Vikings, the strongest run lean in the league. That partly reflects Minnesota's own offense ranking 30th in EPA, which lets opponents lead and lean on the run. The 46.5 total is the lowest of Goff's season and suggests a game without the volume he has been getting.

St. Brown is questionable with an ankle tweak, but Dan Campbell expects him to practice Thursday. His availability matters a lot here, because he is the receiver this defense has struggled with most. Guard Ben Bartch, a 93% snap player, remains on IR until late November. That leaves a weaker interior against the league's best pressure unit, and Goff's 28.2% pressure-to-sack rate ranks only 19th. On Minnesota's side, Aaron Jones is day-to-day, and a limited Vikings offense only reinforces the low-scoring, run-heavy script. The game is indoors.

keyMatchups.title: Interior protection vs league-best pass rush
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota hits the quarterback and sacks him more than anyone. Detroit is without Bartch inside, and Goff turns pressure into sacks at a middling rate. If the pocket collapses before intermediate routes develop, his main source of value disappears.

keyMatchups.title: St. Brown against the one leak
keyMatchups.body: The Vikings have given up real efficiency to opposing WR1s, while shutting down tight ends. A healthy St. Brown is the most likely route to explosive plays. If the ankle limits him, Goff loses his best matchup.

keyMatchups.title: Run-leaning, low-total script
keyMatchups.body: Offenses pass well below normal against Minnesota, and the Vikings' own attack rarely forces a shootout. That points to fewer dropbacks than Goff's usual 37 attempts a game and a passing line well under his season averages.

nextGame.watch: Whether Goff can still complete his intermediate throws when Minnesota brings pressure; if those turn into sacks and checkdowns, expect a sub-250-yard day.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency is built on things that last: a scheme that creates intermediate windows, a deeper and more aggressive throw profile, and LaPorta and Williams as big-play targets. He should stay among the better passers in EPA per dropback, probably closer to his 2024 level than his 2025 one. What won't hold is the interception line. Throwing aggressively at his usual career rates, he should give up picks at something like 0.4-0.7 a game. Yardage should also settle into the 255-295 range once tougher defenses and less frantic scripts arrive.

The Lions' bad defense is the volume floor. As long as it keeps giving up points, Goff will keep throwing, which keeps his yardage and touchdowns high even if efficiency dips. Bartch's return in late November should help protection. A defensive improvement in Detroit would oddly cut into his counting stats while making his job easier.
swingFactors: Whether interceptions arrive as he keeps throwing tight windows
St. Brown's ankle and LaPorta's efficiency holding
How often Detroit's defense forces shootouts

confidence.note: Six games; efficiency matches his 2024 track record, but the zero-INT line and new aggressiveness are short samples.
